headline: Stamp a signature with a time-stamping authority's token, verify the stamp beside the signature it covers, and build the signing-certificate attribute a CAdES signature carries.
summary: A CMS signature can now be taken to the CAdES B-T level: `pki.cms.timestampImprint` produces the imprint a time-stamping authority signs, and `pki.cms.attachTimestamp` splices the returned token into the signature as the signature-time-stamp unsigned attribute. The imprint is the hash of the signature value's contents octets, with neither tag nor length, and the attach verb checks it before writing a byte, so the verb cannot produce a message its own verifier refuses. `pki.cms.verify` reports one row per attached token, each carrying the generation time, the authority and what the authority's chain established, and refuses a token whose time contradicts the signature it stamps. The ESS signing-certificate attribute a CAdES signature must carry has a public builder, and the verdict says which CAdES baseline requirements the signature meets.

Added: `pki.cms.timestampImprint(der, opts?)` returns `{ imprint, signerIndex }` for one signer of a `SignedData`: `imprint` is the `{ hashAlgorithm, hashedMessage }` argument `pki.tsp.request` and `pki.tsp.sign` take, and `signerIndex` the signer it was taken for, which is what `pki.cms.attachTimestamp` is then given. The preimage is the contents octets of that signer's signature OCTET STRING with the tag and length excluded, which is what ETSI EN 319 122-1 clause 5.3 specifies and what RFC 5652 clause 11.4 states for the sibling countersignature. `opts.digestAlgorithm` chooses the digest (`sha256` by default) and `opts.signerIndex` the signer. The digest must be one a timestamp is verified under, so sha256, sha384 and sha512 are admitted and anything else is refused rather than producing an imprint whose token no verifier here would read.

`pki.cms.attachTimestamp(der, token, opts?)` attaches an RFC 3161 `TimeStampToken` as the signature-time-stamp unsigned attribute `{ 1 2 840 113549 1 9 16 2 14 }`. It splices rather than re-signs: the encapsulated content and its type, and per signer the version, the signer identifier, the digest algorithm, the signed attributes, the signature algorithm and the signature, plus every embedded certificate and every attribute already present, are preserved byte for byte. Several tokens may be attached, one per authority, each as its own attribute carrying exactly one value. `opts.signerIndex` names the signer, `opts.pem` returns a PEM block.

`pki.cms.verify` reports `signatureTimeStamps` on each signer, one row per attached token: `{ valid, trusted, genTime, accuracy, serialNumber, policy, revocationChecked, tsa, signer }`, or `{ valid: false, code, message }` where the token does not hold up. A token that fails does not take the signature's own verdict down, since the signature and the time it was made at are separate claims. Each row's imprint is checked against the signature octets the signer verdict was computed over, and a row is refused when its `genTime` precedes the `signing-time` the signature itself asserts or when the latest instant the token could have been created at falls after the signing certificate's `notAfter`, the half of EN 319 122-1 clause 6.3 requirement m that certificate bytes can decide. That bound is the instant the token names plus the accuracy it states, since RFC 3161 section 2.4.2 makes accuracy a window around `genTime` rather than a point, and it keeps the sub-second fraction a `Date` cannot hold. `timestampTrustAnchors`, `timestampCerts` and `timestampRevocationChecker` are the authority's own trust inputs, named apart from the signer's because anchoring a time-stamping authority is a different decision from anchoring a signer.

`pki.cms.verify` reports `cadesBaseline` on each signer, `{ conformant, signingCertificateAttribute, findings, requirementsChecked }`, because a sound signature is not by itself a CAdES signature. The content-type attribute must have value `id-data` (ETSI EN 319 122-1 clause 6.3 requirement f) and the signing certificate must be protected by a `signing-certificate` or `signing-certificate-v2` attribute (clauses 5.2.2.2 and 5.2.2.3). That second requirement is the attribute's claim checked against the certificate the signer resolved to, by the certificate hash and by the issuer and serial where the identifier carries them (RFC 5035 clause 5), not the attribute's presence; a superseded v1 attribute is held to the same claim as the v2 beside it. Each attribute is also held to the digest it binds with, which is what defines the two forms: clause 5.2.2.2 is the attribute using SHA-1 and clause 5.2.2.3 the one using another algorithm, so a v2 identifier binding with SHA-1 is reported against requirement h. Every finding carries the `level` of the requirement it is against and `conformant` answers for the shall-level ones alone, so the two guidance requirements this verdict reads, the issuerSerial field that should not be included (requirement g) and the migration to the v2 form (requirement j), are reported without reading as non-conformance. `requirementsChecked` names the requirements the verdict answered for, so `conformant` is read against that list rather than as a full clause 6.3 audit, and it is reported beside a failed signature rather than withheld.

`pki.schema.smime.buildSigningCertificateV2(certs, opts?)` encodes the ESS `SigningCertificateV2` attribute value (RFC 5035 clause 5.4.1) that binds a signature to the certificate that made it, which is what `openssl cms -verify -cades` requires a signature to carry. `opts.hashAlgorithm` selects `sha256` (the default), `sha384` or `sha512`; SHA-1 is refused, since the verifier reads a SHA-1 binding as a weak one. The SHA-256 form omits the DEFAULT algorithm field and the other two emit the identifier with its parameters field absent.
Changed: `pki.cms.attachTimestamp` refuses a token whose message imprint is a weak digest, and `allowWeakDigests: true` admits it. The verifier refuses such a token by default, so the attach verb holds the same posture rather than writing an attribute whose row would then be refused. An archived token needs the option at both ends.

A time-stamp token whose `hashedMessage` is not the output length of the digest it names is refused as `tsp/imprint-length` rather than `tsp/imprint-mismatch`. The two are different faults: the first says the token is malformed, the second that it is well formed and stamps other bytes. A caller matching on the old code for a length fault reads the new one.
Fixed: The SHA-2 algorithm identifiers `pki.tsp.sign` and `pki.tsp.request` write carried NULL parameters. RFC 5754 section 2 requires an implementation to generate SHA-2 algorithm identifiers with the parameters field absent, which is now what both emit, in the `TSTInfo` message imprint, the `TimeStampReq` message imprint, and the ESS signing-certificate identifier under SHA-384 or SHA-512. Both forms are still accepted on the wire, as that section also requires, and an imprint is matched by the algorithm it names and the digest it carries rather than by the identifier's bytes. The SHA-256 ESS identifier, where the field is the DEFAULT and must be omitted outright, is unchanged.
